questions.q: A student reads "Dry Clean Only" on a garment label and assumes the process uses no liquid at all. What is the fundamental misconception here, and what actually happens during the cleaning stage?
questions.a: The misconception is that "dry" means absence of liquid. In reality, dry cleaning uses liquid organic solvents (e.g., perchloroethylene) — the term "dry" only indicates absence of water. During the cleaning stage, garments are tumbled in a perforated drum while solvent is continuously filtered and circulated, mechanically agitating soils out of the fabric. A wrong answer reveals the student confuses "dry" with "waterless" rather than "non-aqueous."

questions.q: Perchloroethylene (perc) is the most common dry cleaning solvent. Explain why perc effectively removes oily stains from wool but does not cause felting shrinkage, whereas water does.
questions.a: Perc is non-polar and dissolves non-polar oily soils without penetrating the wool fibre's internal structure or swelling the cuticle scales. Water, being polar, hydrogen-bonds with wool's amide groups, causing fibre swelling; mechanical action then makes scales interlock irreversibly (felting). A wrong answer suggests the student thinks perc "coats" fibres or that felting is caused by heat alone, missing the solvent–fibre polarity interaction.

questions.q: A customer brings a rayon challis dress with a grease stain and a "Dry Clean Only" label. The cleaner uses hydrocarbon solvent instead of perc. Is this appropriate? Justify using fibre–solvent–stain interactions.
questions.a: Yes, hydrocarbon solvent is appropriate. Rayon (regenerated cellulose) loses 40–60% tensile strength when wet and is prone to distortion; both perc and hydrocarbon are non-aqueous, but hydrocarbon's lower KB value (solvency power) is sufficient for grease on rayon and is gentler on delicate finishes. Perc's higher solvency could strip certain dyes or finishes on rayon. A wrong answer claims perc is "always better" or that rayon can be wet-cleaned, ignoring wet strength loss.

questions.q: Compare the environmental and health profiles of perchloroethylene vs. liquid CO₂ dry cleaning. Why has perc faced regulatory phase-outs despite its superior cleaning power?
questions.a: Perc is a probable human carcinogen (IARC Group 2A), persistent in groundwater, and requires hazardous waste handling; liquid CO₂ is non-toxic, non-flammable, and leaves zero residue but requires ultra-high-pressure equipment (≈70 bar) and has lower solvency for some polar soils. Regulatory phase-outs (e.g., EPA, California) target perc's occupational exposure and environmental persistence. A wrong answer focuses only on cleaning efficacy or cost, ignoring the toxicological and regulatory drivers.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "All silk garments must be dry cleaned in perchloroethylene." Provide two specific counter-examples with reasoning.
questions.a: The statement is false. Counter-example 1: Silk with water-soluble dyes (e.g., some hand-painted silks) may bleed in perc if the dye has affinity for chlorinated solvents; hydrocarbon or wet cleaning with controlled pH may be safer. Counter-example 2: Lightweight silk chiffon without structure can be professionally wet-cleaned using specialized surfactants and mechanical action control, as per ISO 3175. A wrong answer treats "silk = dry clean" as an absolute rule, ignoring dye–solvent interactions and advances in wet cleaning technology.

questions.q: Design a decision flowchart (text description) that a dry cleaner would use to choose between perc, hydrocarbon, silicone (D5), and liquid CO₂ for an unknown garment with mixed fibre content and unknown stains. Include at least four decision nodes.
questions.a: A good flowchart: Node 1 — Check care label: if "P" (perc allowed) → consider perc; if "F" (hydrocarbon only) → hydrocarbon/D5/CO₂; if "W" (wet clean) → exit dry cleaning. Node 2 — Fibre analysis: acetate/triacetate → avoid perc (can dissolve); spandex/elastane → avoid perc (degrades polyurethane); beaded/sequined → D5/CO₂ (gentle). Node 3 — Stain type: heavy oil/grease → perc/hydrocarbon; water-based stains (sweat, wine) → D5/CO₂ with pre-spotting. Node 4 — Environmental/local regulation: perc banned → hydrocarbon/D5/CO₂. A poor answer lists solvents without decision logic or ignores label symbols and fibre-specific contraindications.
